name: readelf
plain: `readelf` reads a Linux program or library (an ELF file) and prints its structure: the header, the sections, the symbols (names of functions and variables), the protections and more. It never runs the file.
It is the safe first step in a reverse-engineering or binary-exploitation challenge: is it 32 or 64 bit, is it stripped, where are the strings, is the stack executable?
when: First look at a binary: architecture, type, entry point.
Check protections (stack, RELRO) and which libraries it needs.
List function names and find strings in .rodata.

mistakes: Forgetting -W: long lines are cut and symbol names are truncated.
Assuming an empty symbol list means no functions: the binary may be stripped (use objdump -d or a disassembler).
Reading addresses of a position-independent program as final: they are offsets until it is loaded.
Expecting readelf to run or unpack a packed binary: it only shows the file as it is on disk.
try: Find out whether hello is 32 or 64 bit and whether its stack is executable.
Compile hello.c with -static and compare readelf -d.
List the libc functions the program imports.
Strip a binary (strip hello) and compare readelf -s before and after.
see_also: objdump(1), nm(1), file(1), strings(1), ldd(1), checksec, Ghidra and gdb for deeper analysis.
